title: Choose the new composition for the Executive Summary
question: The look does not change and is not on the table: white ground, Somar Sans, tabular numerals, hairline rules, HC red reserved for shortfall and alarm, funding teal for money, green/amber for status. Your four answers are locked in — the page's job is PROMISE vs DELIVERY for one fiscal year; the four coverage percentages keep their exact math but lose their four-equal-cards form; every headline figure carries a delta against the prior year; and planned beneficiaries (men / women / boys / girls) get a first-class section. What is still open is what the page is MADE OF. These three disagree about that: one makes the year itself the structure, one makes the reckoning the structure, one makes the chain the structure. The roll dealt these three and put the first in the lead. Lock one, steer it, or re-roll.

options.label: The Fiscal River
options.lineage: a reservoir hydrograph — inflow and outflow plotted on one shared time axis so the lag between them is a distance you can measure
options.thesis: The year itself is the page: twelve month columns carrying four lanes, where a commitment is drawn at the month it was made and its delivery at the month it landed, so the lag between a promise and its payoff becomes a horizontal gap you can point at instead of a percentage you have to trust.
options.viewport: A single struck-balance line states the year in one sentence. Directly under it, a full-bleed twelve-month band runs edge to edge: lane 1 plans and targets committed, lane 2 money in (per currency, never summed), lane 3 reports due against reports submitted, lane 4 milestones planned against closed. Clicking any month re-scopes the two panels below it — targets vs reported actuals on the start side, money and reach on the end side.
options.case: Refuses the category default outright: no KPI card row, no chart grid. It is the only one of the three that answers WHEN, which is the question a fundraising manager actually gets asked — 'the money came in Q4, that is why Q3 looks bad.' Coverage percentages become a thin rail under the band rather than four boxes.
options.risk: Your data is sparse today (9 annual plans, 9 transfers, 26 reports across the year). A twelve-month river has quiet months, and quiet months must read as deliberate calm rather than as a broken page — that costs real work in the empty states.

options.label: The Commitment Ledger
options.lineage: a double-entry account book opened flat, where nothing is entered on one side without its counterpart on the other
options.thesis: Every figure on the page is half of a pair and none of them is allowed to stand alone: the start column is what this year promised, the end column is what it delivered, and a single continuous variance spine runs down the middle with each row's shortfall struck across it.
options.viewport: A struck-balance sentence, then the spread opens: COMMITTED and DELIVERED as two column heads with the spine between them. Row by row down the page — indicator targets against reported actuals, agreement budgets against cash received (one row per currency), planned beneficiaries against projects and cities live, milestones planned against milestones closed. Each row's gap is drawn on the spine, red when the promise is unmet. The four coverage percentages close the spread as a summary rail.
options.case: The most direct reading of the job you picked: promise vs delivery is not an arrangement here, it is the grammar of every single line. Fastest to scan, hardest to argue with in a board meeting, and it degrades gracefully when a domain has no data.
options.risk: Not every commitment has an honest counterpart — geographic reach has no 'cities promised', so one or two rows must be stated as portfolio-wide facts rather than faked into pairs. A ledger with invented pairs would be worse than no ledger.

options.label: The Strategy Spine
options.lineage: an anatomical plate — one vertebral column with every nerve and vessel traced to the organ it actually serves
options.thesis: The page is the chain itself: one vertical spine running strategy → program → annual plan → target → reported actual, with funding agreements docking in from the side at the exact project they pay for, so the answer to 'what is this money buying' is a line you can follow with a finger.
options.viewport: A struck-balance sentence over a spine rail pinned to the start side. Each program is a node on the spine showing its plan status and target attainment in one bar; opening a node expands its targets against reported actuals in place. Funding agreements enter from the end side as labelled tributaries that connect to the programs they fund, per currency. Beneficiaries and city reach close the spine as its foot.
options.case: The literal answer to 'this is a very important page with many connections.' It is the only card where the relationships are the layout rather than being implied by adjacency, and it is the only one that makes strategy — the top of your hierarchy, currently invisible on this page — carry weight.
options.risk: Fourteen programs on one spine makes a tall page, and depth invites scrolling before understanding. The head of the spine has to answer 'is this year on track' completely, before anything is expanded — if it does not, this becomes a navigation tree wearing a diagram's clothes.
